text:
Oh you, who subdue me. Why have you arrived late?
Why have you come now, when the soul does not burn,
when I have no roses with which to make you
a joyful garland sprinkled with stars?


Oh you, whose word is sweet as the murmur
of fountain water; sweet as the cooing
of the turtledove; sweet as sleeping kisses
upon two pale hands that protect nests.


Oh you, who with your hands can take my head
and make flowers spring from it like a tree in festival
and make a smile arch between my lips
like a cloudy sky that suddenly iridesces.


Why have you arrived late? Why have you come now
when I have been vanquished by a destroying flame,
when I have been swept away by divine fire
and go, blinded and sad, along a black road?


I want, God of gods, to be made wholly new.
Let them weave me with lilies; let the hands of mystery
prune me; let them strip away my weeds.
Your lips were not made to cure sorrow.


For your lips, water of supreme purity.
For your lips, crystal cups and the pure-white foam
of a soul that knows nothing of bees,
nor of honeys, nor of crimson flowers.


For your hands, those that have never shrouded;
for your eyes, those that have never wept;
for your dreams, dreams like golden swans;
so that your pupils might pursue my traces,


Oh, if my petals then, crushed by your hands,
were to acquire superhuman powers by magic
and, made light, cling to the light of the stars
so that your pupils might pursue my traces.


Welcome the death you would give me by drinking me in;
welcome your fire that withers springs;
welcome your fire that kills the rosebushes:
let every corolla draw near your evils.


Oh you, whom I idolize above existence,
oh you, for whom I desire my essence renewed.
Why have you come now, when I will not achieve
the divine torment of seeing myself unpetaled?...

translation.title: Oh, You!
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the apostrophe’s repeated “Oh you,” its floral imagery, and the final paradox of renewal through being stripped of petals.
